reviewText: This is a fun and simple game for anyone eight and up, although I think you need to be at least nine in order to play the game with any real strategy.  Children younger than eight can play it, if they like playing new board games.I won't repeat what the other reviews said -- most of them are pretty accurate.  If you're looking for a new game that your whole family can play, this is a good choice.  I would recommend this game for adults only if they're not hard-core board game players.So let me just talk about the problems with this game.There is very little interaction among players.  You could carve out an area of the board and just play within that area, building higher and higher.  The taller your building is, the faster you will get more points.  In fact, interacting with other players is penalized, because other players get a bonus if you build on top of their buildings.  This game is pretty boring with only two players -- you really need to have four.The use of paper money is odd, since you cannot use your earned money to buy anything.  The money is used just as a scoring system.  But because it's made from thin paper, it damages easily.  I recommend you build a tuck box to store the paper.The box itself is also bad at storing pieces.  Each player gets a colored box to store the blocks and the tiles, but these boxes are barely large enough to hold everything.  The box that holds the money, however, is much too large.The worst thing about this game, however, is the manual.  There are errors in the rules that make it hard to understand.  I recommend that you download the alternate English translation from boardgamegeek.com, because it's much better.  The instructions also talk about how the various colors interact, but the manual is printed in black-and-white, so you can't actually see what they're talking about.
summary: A fun and simple family game, but the manual is bad

The wood is solid, the colors are vibrant and look great despite some rough use (i.e. throwing). The pictures of the animals haven't chipped or ripped.-The nice thing about these is the magnet is a thin sheet that is attached to the entire surface of the animal (unlike those little plastic letters that just have a little magnet attached to the back). This is a key feature, because that means these letters won't scratch surfaces (i.e. your stainless steel fridge!). My son mainly uses them on his easel but has wandered into the kitchen with them and I don't have to worry about him putting them on the fridge.

reviewText: Although designed for 2-4 year olds, our 15 month old has enjoyed using the Tag.  Once you get the Tag set up, it's easy to use.  To use the Tag, you press its base against each page of the included books and the device reads the text.  The books in this set are designed around each of the vowell sounds, a-e-i-o-u and use simple and fun characters.  This is not a substitute for reading to your kids, but I would think it wouldn't hurt as an additional way to teach them to read.  Now, the downside is that the Tag memory does not come ready to go.  You have to connect it to the internet and download the content for each book.  It is tedious but not too difficult to figure out.  The other downside is that the memory is limited.  So, the device won't hold the content for all the books that come with the set.  Despite the negatives, this is a neat idea and something fun and educational for kids.
summary: Nice Educational Toy but with a Few Negatives

reviewText: This is my second RC heli. I bought the first, an Execuheli, on impulse when I saw it on sale in a dept. store for which I had a $10 off anything over $10 coupon, and so the Execuheli only cost me $6. Long story short, IMO $6 is all the Execuheli is worth. After reading reviews on Amazon and elsewhere of other RC helis suitable for indoor use by beginners, and watching video reviews and demonstrations, I decided to try the Syma S107. At the current price of around $20, it's a steal. Mine worked perfect the first time I used it (after charging it via USB for about 30 minutes). It could be faster (though there are ways to modify it that are said to increase speed), and as others note, the recharge time is on the long side (e.g., the Execuheli recharges in about 10 minutes). But for the current price, I would say this is nitpicking. It is a plus that it can be recharged via USB with the included cable, because that saves on the lives of the six AA batteries that power the remote. I've crashed mine quite a few times with zero signs of damage. I may buy more to give as holiday gifts, and if I do I will supply batteries for the remotes and will pre-charge (and test) the helis so that the recipient can start having fun right away.

reviewText: I’m a huge gamer.  But honestly I’m more of a theme gamer.  I love Dominion not just for its art and great mechanics, but also for its fantastic theme.  Same with Sail to India.  So games like this don’t really get me super interested at first.  That’s because it might have a lot of strategy but it’s light on theme.But this game is pretty great actually.  It’s simple to learn.  Draw a card.  Play up to two.  If it’s a 5 of diamonds, play a peg on a red five.  A queen of spades, play it on a black queen square.  Play two of a kind (suit doesn’t matter) and you get to place two pegs anywhere on the board!  Play a run of the same suit (4, 5; 2, 3; Jack, queen; etc.) and you remove two pegs.  To win you just need to complete a path across the board.If I had one complaint it would be that the blue and purple pegs have the same type of hue.  So it can make it difficult to differentiate in low light.  Still that’s a very minor complaint.The game is simple and plays fast.  Most ages would be able to understand this game.  And it’s very entertaining.  I recommend it to groups who want a light weight but very replayable game.Weight: Light  Strategy: Medium  Replayability: Medium to High

reviewText: This is a nice puzzle that offers can occupy a child for a while, provided a child has enough patience, or serve as a quick child-parent game.  Puzzle pieces are made of thick plastic, they fit snugly, and the completed puzzle is sturdy.  The puzzle comes with a display stand.  The puzzle is about as challenging as a LEGO set, because both provide instructions on what to do.My 4 1/2 year old son and I put this puzzle together in about 30 minutes.  In the beginning I was sorting pieces and he was assembling the puzzle.  All pieces are numbered and have directional arrows showing where the next piece goes.  It was pretty easy for my son to assemble to piece #100, at which point he started looking for piece #200 because he only knew how to count in hundreds past 100.  So, I explained to him that after 100 comes 101, which I thought to be a nice teaching moment.By this point, I have already sorted all pieces and arranged them in groups of ten.  I began assembling the puzzle beginning with the piece #130 and up.  When my son installed piece #129, we joined the part he was assembling with the part that was assembled by me and then quickly finished the remaining 20 or so pieces.The result was a pretty colorful and sturdy ball showing a picture of the NY Times Square at night.
summary: Fun to put together with a child

reviewText: There are three water color boards in this package.  We got the kit with dolphins.  The "canvas" is set up with clear lines that delineate the shapes of what you are painting.  If you used paint by numbers as a kid - this will have a similar feel to it.  There are several great things about this kit.  First, the paint is really high quality water color - I know because I order art supplies all the time and these paints were better than what I order from the school supply warehouses.  They come in convenient little bottles that drop or stream - depending on how hard you squeeze.  Five stars for paint quality and pigment.  The booklet has a fantastic color chart and recipe page - easy to follow - kids loved creating the different blends.  And there is a GREAT explanation of about half a dozen water color painting techniques - explained in a paragraph for each one - and a color example of what it looks like, i.e., glazing.I brought this out to a local park, we used the water from the park - nothing special and we sat at a picnic table and worked with this for about two hours.  It was an AMAZING experience.  The kids stayed focused (8 and 10 years old), they talked about everything (which was priceless to me) and my son has an incredible painting ability - who knew?!?  He never sits long enough to demonstrate any talent - until I saw this.  We laughed and joked and poked fun at our work - some of the color choices - and it was great fun.Tips:  Bring additional fine brushes - the kit only comes with one very nice two sided brush - you will actually need about 6 water color - 5 point or so - brushes.  You may want to bring a bigger one for the larger areas.  Also, bring a microfiber cloth to wipe the brushes.  The kit does come with a blotting paper - but how easy is a microfiber cleaning cloth?!  And I brought three extra cups for clear water to continuously rinse the brushes.  And another cup for clear painting water for glazing the picture, etc.  Leave in the air to dry - depending on how saturated the paint (water) soaks the paper, you do need some drying time.  One last thing - you can use empty foam egg crates for additional painting stations.  The kit comes with a fantastic little plastic paint receptacle for mixing and dipping, but you may want more than one and empty egg crates are perfect for this.I only wish there were 5 or more painting sheets in each box, because it would be a PERFECT party activity, and a few more paintbrushes.
summary: Discovered my son has some artistic talent

reviewText: When this arrived, my 7 year old daughter knew immediately what they were. Bakugan for girls, she says they're called at school. They're bright, colorful and seemed designed to appeal to girls who love Littlest Pet Shop or My Little Pony Ponyville figures. That being said, I'd recommend them for the slightly older 6+ rather than 5 and up the packaging states. The ears, tails, flippers etc. seem rather flimsy and it doesn't seem like it'd take much to break or smash one of these little fellows. We haven't had any problems with eyes not opening or closing, but as other reviewers have mentioned, it's best to tuck in the extra bits before closing them into the ball shape. They are cute, but for the price, it seems like there should be more included. The bag does zipper tight and seems like it'd be a good place to keep everything in one place. Overall, I don't understand the appeal, but then, I'm not the target audience. My daughter loves them and has had a lot of fun creating stories and adventures for her set. They do encourage imaginative play and don't make any loud, annoying noises so that's definitely a plus.

reviewText: The box in which Chuggington's Wooden Railway Over and Under Starter Kit is packaged boasts that the railway is made of "real wood," and includes both Wilson and Koko. Who or what is Wilson? Who or what is Koko? The trains? The ones whose faces are on the trains? I don't know and it doesn't matter. This play set, as I think it would be called, is recommended for ages "3+," but I doubt the plus is meant to include anyone in my, shall we say, "advanced" age group.I gave this to my niece's three-year-old, and though he's rather articulate for his age, he refused my request for an interview. I can only assume he likes it. I didn't play with it myself, but I will say this is a high quality item with plastic that looks and feels quite durable, and, as noted, tracks made from genuine wood. There are 22 pieces (and more can be purchased separately) with two train engines, someone or something called Vee, a Clock Tower Tunnel, a Bridge Tunnel, and track pieces. Depending on the child's skill and imagination, he/she can construct this railway in a variety of ways and have a lot of fun doing it. This is a cool toy.Highly recommended.Brian W. Fairbanks

reviewText: I got this for my granddaughter, age 27 months, and had it shipped directly to her. Then I forgot to tell my daughter I'd done that, so the gift arrived as a total surprise with no comment from me--and they loved it!!! My granddaughter enjoys the toy immensely despite being a bit younger than the recommended age range for it, and after a bit of play has learned to direct the truck more or less as she likes.Why did this toy appeal to me so much? The way we interact with our world is changing daily because of advances in technology. As a computer instructor, I see the tremendous difference in the speed with which students acquire new skills based on whether the basic means of interaction is familiar and intuitive, or something altogether new. I think the wand interface on this toy will develop the kinds of foundation skills that will help my granddaughter master a great deal of essential technology when she's a little older, much the way that people who knew how to type had an advantage when computers became ubiquitous, and those who already know how to use a mouse have a head start toward mastering Microsoft Office. The fire truck wand reminds me of interfaces I'm seeing become more popular today (such as the nifty things people are doing with Kinect), and I want my granddaughter to have every advantage I can give her.Besides, the fire truck's antics bring about regular belly laughs and are great fun!!!

reviewText: I've played Bananagrams with a number of different players, and ultimately, I must say that the game is fun, but there are some issues. The short advice is that if you like word games (like Scrabble), you'll probably like Bananagrams.The game itself is pretty straight forward. Each player takes a number of tiles (somewhere between 16-20 tiles each), and then the game starts. You must take your tiles and start forming words in a crossword puzzle style. After someone has used all of their tiles, they yell "Banana" and everyone grabs an extra tile to work into their crossword puzzle. The game continues until all tiles have been taken, and the first to finish then is the winner.The problems with this game come into play when trying to mesh in with it's audience. If someone is really good at this game, it tends to be impossible for any other player to win. If a player happens to get a good set of letters and finishes their initial set quickly, then they tend to keep yelling banana until the game ends. Likewise, when you get behind it's very difficult to get back in the game. These problems occasionally ruin the game, but players tend to get used to this.The bright side is that bananagrams is also a pretty free form game. It can work with a number of players (even 1), could easily be played in teams, could be played as one giant crossword rather than 1 crossword per player, and with some additional thought, more alternative game types could be created (maybe even something as simple as "nouns only").Overall, the fast gameplay and free form nature of the game help it appeal to a wide group. Don't expect this game to last you all night long, but it's great as a more casual event where everyone can participate.

It really is a neat toy and brings lots of joy to my son, so I think its a great product.  Usually these toys get played with for a day and then the kid is bored of it, but my son is still playing with it and enjoying it.This isn't a very educational toy, but it does spark an interest in learning more about dinosaurs, so I like it.

reviewText: I've seen these products around for years but had always noted the generally poor reviews and stayed away. How sad for us that we've gone so long without Moon Dough! I will state first off, there are two brands of this type of "dough" which are usually lined up right next to each other in your local toy section. Moon Dough and Moon Sand are NOT the same thing, even though the packaging and toy itself is very similar. I have never bought Moon SAND, so I won't talk about that here, but it was the first of these types of toys to arrive on the market and the ones I have always seen with the poor reviews.Ok, so we've had Play-doh since my oldest son (5) was a toddler. There's just something irresistible about gooey, colorful dough that kids can't seem to go without out. We have quite a number of the little Play-doh sets, totaling a few hundreds dollars, I'm sure. Though they always seemed really exciting at first, they always lead to inevitable disappointment and boredom when they can't make the items and creatures look like they do on the box. It's too hard to get all those different colors to look right and even harder to just get the Play-Doh out of the molds most of the time. Moon Dough doesn't pretend that your child can make all these detailed, multi-colored animals. It shows you right on the box, these animals are one color and even your youngest child can make them without any help, and that's where the real fun is. My son who normally gets bored/frustrated within 10 minutes of Play-Doh can play with Moon Dough for several hours, on and off throughout the day. If I leave it on the kitchen table all day, he will absolutely return to it several times and play independently for long periods.Things I (as Mom) love about Moon Dough, it never dries out! Literally. We tried! We left some Moon Dough out on the kitchen table the first week we had it just to see if it changed in any way. Nope! I can't say how much I love this after having Play-Doh all these years. When the kids are done with Play-Doh, you have to pack it up right then. I keep a clean house, but I don't always have the convenience of stopping everything I'm doing to pick up Play-Doh which always seems to take ages to locate all the bits and pieces that have scattered around and become embedded into things. This leads me to my next point. Moon Dough doesn't stick to anything! Sure, a little will get on your clothes during play, but it brushes right off. Yes, some will get on the floor and be scattered around. But if the floor is clean, just sweep up the Moon Dough and put it back in the bag. It doesn't stick to the broom and it's still good for play. Try that with Play-Doh! I also really appreciate the lack of odor with Moon Dough. Some people love that Play-Doh smell, and I am not one of them. It gives me a headache nearly every time I'm in close quarters with it. Moon Dough has a very faint smell and you can only really notice it if you've got it right up under your nose. On top of that, the dough is very soft and being that it doesn't stick on anything, it doesn't stick up under my fingernails like Play-Doh. That's always a plus!What do my kids love about Moon Dough? My 5-year-old can play completely independently. He can make all the animals by himself, and they always come out perfectly. All he has to do is push the dough in the hole at the top of the barn until it's full, and turn the handle. Out pops a cute, perfectly formed critter. The animals once made are delicate to play with, but so are ones made from Play-Doh. Play-Doh creations can wilt and sag over time as well, but not with Moon Dough. Their little animals can sit out for hours and days. Unless my son is trying to squish them, they'll probably be fine. He knows they are GI Joe and knows to be gentle with them. But when he's ready to make something new, he sticks them back in the pile and the fun continues. I've watched him make little fences to surround his barn, hay for his horses to eat, and now we have the puppy set as well which lets him make bowls, bones and treats for his pups. I'm always amazed at how with so little effort the molds always come out with such detail. With a child of this age and equal effort, you're lucky if you can even come up with something recognizable with Play-Doh. Add onto that the fact that we can use all our old Play-Doh molds with Moon Dough and we're ready to pack up Play-Doh for good. I would NOT, however, use Play-Doh with the Moon Dough barn or doghouse because it will become stuck and gunk up the toy.The only, ONLY, downside I can see to Moon Dough is that you can't really sculpt free form with it. It just doesn't work because it will crumble as you try to shape it with your hands. I don't really see this as a downside for younger children because all they want to do is use the molds anyway. For older children, maybe 7+, who want to actually try to sculpt something, Play-Doh is superior. But at that point, you should probably just get your child some real clay and let them make something they can keep. (We've tried making Play-Doh creations for keeping, it doesn't work, they completely fall apart even when hard.)I'll break it down into pros and cons for those of you still on the fence.Pros-----Durable-Never dries out-Easy clean up-No smell-Works with Play-Doh molds-Kids can do it independently-Non-toxic and hypoallergenicCons-----No sculptingThis seems like a long review for such a simple toy, but I really want to emphasize how strongly I feel that Moon Dough is the superior product for younger children. I wish we had this years ago and the reason we didn't was because of all the negative reviews. Don't take my word for it, go pick up one of the small sets and try it out. They're very affordable.
summary: Moon dough deserves it's place next to Play-Doh!

For older children, maybe 7+, who want to actually try to sculpt something, Play-Doh is superior. But at that point, you should probably just get your child some real clay and let them make something they can keep. (We've tried making Play-Doh creations for keeping, it doesn't work, they completely fall apart even when hard.)I'll break it down into pros and cons for those of you still on the fence.Pros-----Durable-Never dries out-Easy clean up-No smell-Works with Play-Doh molds-Kids can do it independently-Non-toxic and hypoallergenicCons-----No sculptingThis seems like a long review for such a simple toy, but I really want to emphasize how strongly I feel that Moon Dough is the superior product for younger children. I wish we had this years ago and the reason we didn't was because of all the negative reviews. They're very affordable.

reviewText: The concept of Ravensburger's "Penguin Pile-up" is a fun one - place the penguins onto an "iceberg" until one or more falls off.  If you cause the spill, then you add the fallen penguins to your colony.  The winner is the player who places all their penguins and has none remaining.  Reading is not required; everyone, adults included, can have an enjoyable time with "Penguin Pile-up."  Suggested for ages 5 and older, "Penguin Pile-up" can be played by younger children once they have an understanding of taking turns.  My three-year old grandson burst into peals of laughter the first time penguins toppled off the iceberg.I liked the fact that children can begin to learn about balancing items and have to think about placing penguins on the "iceberg."  Without seeming complicated , "Penguin Pile-up" introduces strategic thinking to children.  They must determine where to place their own penguins in order to maximize the chance an opponent will topple the birds.However, the quality of "Penguin Pile-up's" construction leaves something to be desired.  It is definitely not up to Ravensburger's usually high standards.  The "iceberg" is constructed of two pieces of brittle, flimsy plastic.  The edges are rough and might easily cut tender skin.The penguins consist of three separate, small pieces which must be assembled before one can use them.  Families having very young children or children who tend to put things in their mouth may want to avoid this game for that reason.I would have preferred to pay more for the game so the penguins were each one solid piece, and so the "iceberg" was constructed of better materials and was more smoothly finished.  I have awarded "Penguin Pile-up" only 4 stars because of its lesser quality when compared to other Ravensburger products.

reviewText: The first thing you'll notice about this game, is how wonderfully well-made it is. I was blown away just by the quality of the snails, and how durable the board is. You are able to purchase extra characters to catch the Goblin.

reviewText: My son received this at 19 months and is 22 months now. He plays with this table, but usually we just pull out the bag of Mega Blok Legos without the table. We are able to build a bigger variety of things with the bag of 200 Mega Legos when not using the table. The road takes up much of the building room, so I would have preferred it not have the road in the middle. If we didn't already have a 200 count bag of Mega Bloks and a million other toys, maybe my son would have played with this one more. It could be that the 20 bloks included in this set are enough to keep the attention of little ones when they don't have a bunch of other options to choose from.If you are short on storage room, then you'll probably like that this table can fold up when it is not in use. You won't be able to fit additional Mega Bloks in this table for storage though, so don't throw away what you are currently storing your Mega Legos in. I noticed some people complained their child removed the stickers, but so far mine hasn't. In my opinion, it does not matter if the stickers are on the legos or not so that should not be a deciding factor on purchasing this table or not. If there's a Mega Blok table without the road, go that direction before buying this one. Overall, I love Mega Bloks. This table did include several legos that are not included in the 80 and 200 count bags (i.e. bridges, car, etc).

reviewText: As a puzzle enthusiast who's done many puzzles through the years I'd probably say Ravensburger has the best quality puzzles. Like this one, the edges are all crisply cut and the quality of the print is good.This 1000 piece Times Square puzzle is one of their best 1000 piece I've ever done. I think the picture is superb. It's a busy picture with lots going on as Times Square always is. Colors are bright and beautiful and most of it is non-repeating, so despite the size, it's not too hard to do.The new wrinkle here is the Augmented Reality app. This is something you can download for free to your i device. And after you download it you hold it over your puzzle to get additional audio/visual activity. You can watch the scene animate, get more information on the scene and even see your own pic on the billboard. I think this AR function is a lot of fun. For the first time, it isn't just a static puzzle, there are things you can do with it once you're finished. Now I'm kinda wishing all puzzles are like that.Overall, another quality Ravensburger puzzle. A 1000 piece that's not hard to do and comes with an AR function that allows you to play with it. Adn the price is about the same as a 1000 piece Ravensburger without the AR, so I think it's a great deal. Highly recommended.

reviewText: It is a bit difficult to understand just what this product is, but Crayola has a nice video explaining it in the product images.  In the pack is the Light Designer, which has two clear removable plastic drawing boards, and four gel markers.  The latter give a neon look and wash off surprisingly easily with just warm water.  So, what do you do with this thing?Since the drawing boards are removable, they can be placed on a picture (or face) to trace it.  Want to draw something from scratch?  The clear boards still come in handy, since you can trace your own work and create a basic two-frame animation, similar to what you might do by flipping between two pieces of paper.  The Light Designer takes the work out of it by automatically lighting up alternating boards.  The effect is pretty good, though it works best in a very dark room.This toy is probably going to be used a lot for a little while, then forgotten, but the price is not bad for the entertainment it provides.  It might even spark some interest in art that will grow over time.

reviewText: What a fabulous toy to encourage imaginative play!  I have a 5-year old son and a 4-year old daughter, and both spent a good afternoon playing with this playset when they first got it.  Even after a few days, they're still playing with it a lot, and even integrated theFisher-Price Imaginext DC Super Friends Batcave (Frustration-Free Packaging), theFisher-Price Imaginext Dragon World Fortress, and theFisher-Price Imaginext DC Super Friends Green Lantern Planet OAplaysets into the fun.There's a lot to like about Action Tech City:1.  It's highly interactive.  Seriously, this thing is not the tallest Imaginext Set we own, and individually each piece is as wide as the Batcave and Dragon Fortress.  However, when linked together, it's the widest, and if you place both on top of each other, it's as tall as the Batcave and D.Fortress.  The biggest advantage this playset has over BC and DF is that it has the most activities for kids to engage in.  There's an elevator, multiple doors to open and shut, a bank to break into, fires that pop up at a turn of a dial and that "go out" when you tap the flames...seriously, there's a LOT to play with on this toy.2.  The speech and sound are loud - but not blaring loud - and very very clear.  The other playsets we own don't have this sound clarity, and this many phrases.  Best part, it's triggered by the Fire Engine, so the kids don't have to look for a button to push on the playset itself.  The reception is about as far as a television remote (about 15-20 ft max).3.  The Action Tech City folds down small.  This may not be a big issue for some, but I like having things tucked away neatly when not in use.  These two playsets, because they're connected in the center, fold together back to back for easy storage.  There is, however, no real place to tuck away all the additional little pieces.  If you have a ziploc bag, or at least a designated place to put the mini figures, weapons, water pieces, and so forth in, then you'll be set.4.  There are a lot of little pieces to play with that are compatible with other Imaginext Playsets.  The kids have a good time interchanging where the pieces go.  I'll sometimes find a fire hydrant on the firehouse roof and the street lamps dangling from the flag poles or also on the roof.  Recently, I've found a satellite dish on the Dragon Fortress and street lamps popping up around the Batcave.  This is a big plus knowing that all the accessories and figures can work with other playsets (with exception of the IR elements like that on the firetruck).There are very few things that I dislike about this set - the only thing I didn't like was the fact that this playset did have a lot of little pieces.  Little piece to step on.  At midnight.  In bare feet.  But that may not be an issue to you - and if anything, may be good training when your kids start playing with the toys that really hurt to step on, like Legos or My Little Pony hairbrushes.  There's only two pieces that would really be missed if lost, and that's the two "water pieces" that fit into the truck.  These two pieces can be shot from the Firetruck, and without them, there's no "water" to shoot.  They're pretty big, so hopefully they won't get lost.If you're interested in expanding on this particular playset, you can purchase theFisher-Price Imaginext Rescue City Dix Big Rig,Fisher-Price Imaginext Rescue City Police Car,Fisher-Price Imaginext Rescue City Tow Truck, and theFisher-Price Imaginext Rescue City Ambulance.  The Rescue City Center recognizes these four vehicles and will respond with different speech and sound.  There is a firetruck already included in case you're not interested in expanding just yet.All in all, this playset, even when played by itself, is a HUGE winner.  With lots to do, lots of pieces included, and two mini figures to share, this definitely will keep your kids busy for a while.  Highly recommended!

reviewText: I picked this up based on the Scrabble name alone and as you may have already read in other reviews this handheld has little (i.e. Nothing!) to do with the traditional game of Scrabble. This is the simple game of 'what word or phrase am I thinking' and it does the job admirably. It's a team game so your goal is to get your partner to guess correctly without you using any of the desired words. So your aim is not to stump someone - it's to help without 'cheating' then pass it to the next team for their go and as such it only works with a minimum of four people so do keep that in mind.  But that's the fun I think - it's a party game, one to drag out after a few saucy drinks and throw down some word skills for a little while. Which is exactly what we did.The unit itself is much bigger than I expected. I was anticipating something like the little 20Q handhelds but this is about 8-10 inches tall and this aids in its durability and also the larger screen and buttons help.So - a great inexpensive fun guess-the-word game that takes all the scoring chores away leaving you to simply play and have fun with adult(ish!) friends. Enjoy it this holiday season.
summary: Fun game - but for four or more...

reviewText: Probably most of us played Connect 4 as kids.  It's a fun strategy game and little ones also love it when you drop all of the pieces out and they come tumbling down.  This version is definitely a valuable update to the old classic.  It's colorful and exciting enough to engage kids, but fun for parents to play as well.  Plus, it has the added excitement of the launchers, and we all know kids love it when anything goes flying.  It's definitely weighted more towards chance than the older game.  The original Connect 4 was really about strategy, but in this, with the addition of the launchers, there is more uncertainty (although it's not too hard to aim them where you want them to go).  This is a hit in our house and I imagine lots of families will enjoy it.

reviewText: This game had already been out for over a year before I decided to buy it for my 10-year old grandson.  I was familiar with the premise and the gameplay, and knew he'd love it.  What I didn't know is how much my daughter would enjoy playing the game with him. (She's not that much into games).  When I finally got around to playing it with him, I was hooked.Yes, this is a fun dice game with a cool B-movie monster smackdown theme.  There are two ways to win - either be the first to score 20 Victory points or be the last monster standing.  As in Yahtzee, you roll a set of dice (six in this game) up to three times, keeping the ones you want and re-rolling the rest. The dice faces have the numbers 1, 2, and 3, a lightning bolt, a heart, and a monster's claw.  If you match three of a single number, you gain that many Victory points.  For each lightning bolt, you get a small green cube, which you can collect to buy power-up cards with.  Each heart will help to heal you, giving you one hit point back.  And each claw is a successful attack on one of your enemies.Tokyo only has room for one monster (well, two if you have 5-6 players).  When one monster is in the city, everyone else battles against him until he leaves or gets killed.  It's a simple premise, but SO MUCH FUN.  The power-up cards - some that have lasting abilities and some that are played immediately, add some hilarious variety to this game,  And with a playtime that usually runs inside a half-hour, you WILL want to play it again and again.I'm contemplating adding a copy to my own collection so I can play with my adult friends.  It's that good!!!!
summary: More fun than a Godzilla movie

reviewText: My four year old now has about ten of these hardcover books to go with his Tag Reader pen, and not one of them has yet to get old.  He still uses the sample book that came with the pen, for that matter.  It really is a fun learning device.So much so that as I got the book and pen to go through the book to review it, he grabbed them from me and he's now exploring Monster's University yet again.  It might help that we took him out to see the movie this week, and he had a great time watching Monster's University in the theater.If you're not familiar with LeapFrog's LeapReader, it's a very easy to use, lightweight, pen-shaped reader which interprets text and images from LeapFrog books, then narrates what you've selected.  It also gives you fun tasks to perform; asking you to go find something throughout the book, or in the case of Monster's University, asking you to create your own monster.You do have to establish an account with LeapFrog where you can download each book's software to the pen.  The pen allows you or your child to read the stories or play the games, and as the pen stores only a certain amount of books in its memory, this account includes a library where you can select which books you can keep on your pen.Specifically regarding this Monster's University, there is the aforementioned Create Your Own Monster game as well as a "Where's Waldo" style game where you have to find several monsters one at a time from a large university classroom. Several pages throughout the book also have game icons which, when pressed, ask trivia questions about the story.  One non-game activity has Sully teaching a class on the verbs and nouns of scaring methods.  The games have two levels of difficulty, and once the first levels have been mastered, the "level twos" are available.Of course, the main thing about the book is that you can click on one icon, and a very pleasant voice reads the whole book to you.  Or, you can choose to have that same voice read you one page at a time.  Or the best part to me; the pen allows you to read one word at a time, so when your little boy or girl is trying to read it on their own, they can use the pen to help them out as the go along.  What's that word?  Point at it.  Slide over it.  The word is revealed.  They can do this with Mom or Dad right there, or if they're busy, they can do it themselves.  It's a great concept.I give this book (as I would, most likely, all books for this product) 4.5 stars, and that .5 star is taken off only because I think this product will only get better.  I highly, highly recommend, for Monster's U and for the Tag Reader.

reviewText: The Complete Kids Campfire is one of a number of products designed to allow children to pretend they're camping - even when inside. Other items from the product manufacturer  include indoor tents, lanterns, and more.I've always loved toys like these ( toy drills or ovens are other examples) which are springboards for kids' imagination. Television and video games have their place, too, but children who have a chance to enact their own adventures...including camping...are lucky indeed.With the Complete Kids Campfire, aspiring campers can gather their "supplies" and go camping inside - even on the coldest, snowiest days. It can sometimes be a challenge to find unique toys that appeal to kids. The campfire kit fills that gap. It does, however,have one feature I'd like changed -a motor noise from a built- in fan. And that noise could be a deal breaker.For potential buyers who might worry that even a safe, artificial (but very realistic looking) campfire could encourage children to play with fire, I'd argue the opposite. Instead, this toy provides the perfect opportunity to discuss fire safety. The enclosed product literature even has link to a U.S. Fire Administration (USFA) website page focused on educating both parents and children about basic fire safety. Impressive!. The website is also noted on the package itself.As for the toy campfire, here's a quick rundown of the major features:Pros:1. Realistic "flame" created by a wispy, flame-shaped fabric which moves just like the flickering orange glow of a fire (with the help of a battery-powered fan concealed in the toy).2. The campfire is packaged in a box with an orange background, perfect for using as back drop to make the "fire" look very awesome and even more spectacular.3. Even kids living in city apartments or homes far from the country can pretend they're camping. Now all kids, city or country dwellers, can play at camping...no matter what the weather.4. Ready to use  right out of the package, complete with batteries. Nothing extra to buy.5. As noted before, an excellent toy for pretend play, offering a great option to television and a way to relieve boredom when bad weather prevents outside play....if the noise factor can be ignored..the motor sound.7. Can be used by more than one child at a time or with parents who want to get in on the fun.Cons:I have only one suggestion to take this product from fun to phenomenal...get rid of the noisy motor sound and substitute something that simulates a crackling fire.

reviewText: I have been searching for a long time for the one game, so vile, so funny, and so adult like that it seems like I have been searching forever. One day, I get wind of this game called Cards Against Humanity which apparently would fill that void in my every Friday adult game night routine. Naturally I contact the CAH team about a review, and they sent me the base game along with the 1st-3rd expansion's.Honestly, no matter which way you play it, the entire setup cannot get any easier; assuming that you know how to properly deal cards of course. When TheGamingExperience members got together and played (almost daily), we sat around a table and I dealt out the cards (we played with 7 people), and then it was non-stop fun.Setup is the exact same for the expansions as well.The great thing about the design of Cards Against Humanity is that it takes everything that adult life has to offer and makes a huge play on them. I will not say that design is perfect, because there are... some questionable cards; just a couple that don't make sense. Not that they are bad cards (there...are...um...some...disturbing ones) a couple were just too advanced for us in terms of understanding. This actually works in the games favor though, as I want cards I do not fully understand, cards that do not make sense to me but might to someone else.When the team and I had first played it, we did one of the suggestions; we played with a player named Rando. Rando though is not your average Cards Against Humanity player, he/she/it has the most disturbing mind out of anyone that played. Just an an example, on the question card was something to the effect of "What was Micheal Jacksons last thought before he died?" While most of us went the not-so-obvious way, Rando threw down the "Pedophile" card; we almost all died laughing at this huge coincidence. Of course there are many other ways to play Cards Against Humanity but this was the best (and funniest) way we found.Playability is honestly one of Cards Against Humanity's downfall; while it is somewhat high, it does  get very repetitive. However, with the addition of the expansions (rather cheap for price too), it lightens the game up quite a bit if you want more cards. We played so much, we knew most of the cards in the base game, so we threw in the 1st expansion which really livened it up a bit; effectively giving us something to look forward to. Subsequent playthroughs we utilized each of the 3 expansions and it really made things much more enjoyable.In conclusion, Cards Against Humanity is a REALLY fun game, that brings with it non-stop laughter. reviewText: Most kids of a certain generation had the original Simon Says game.  Dinner-plate sized, heavy, and very battery-consumptive, but fun nonetheless as a memory game.  It also had that 'Close Encounters' association, so I used to imagine communicating with aliens as I played...The variations of the original game go to either key-chain sized minis, or significantly more expensive variations.  Simon flash is most likely a better value than either, because the original is there, but it is not the only game.  Each of the four games are intuitive and amusing; I played the basic game with a six y.o., who took to it immediately, and the others with a couple of 8 y.o.'s who were also greatly captivated.  The small size and light weight make this an on-the-go possibility as well.A few downsides however; the "bits" are four identically-sized cubes.  Each requires 2 AA batteries.  I've not gotten through a set yet, but light and sound generators are accompanied by proximity sensors which measure the location and i.d. of the next cube, so there must be some power consumption here; batteries could become a significant cost.The other is that the original game allows the use of a two-part yellowish 'shell' for keeping the individual cubes together (also a good way to store the game), but the others involve moving the cubes around.  They seem to work best with pretty careful and close alignment, which the 8 y.o.'s found annoying.  I imagine the game working best on a music stand or other slanted surface that directs alignment.This would be a good choice for a birthday present for a 7-10 y.o., or even a good game for a senior as a memory-retention tool.  And it still allows us to pretend we're communicating with aliens.

reviewText: My previous review described the wrong product, so here is the correct one.My kidlets, ages 4 and 7 enjoyedColor Bloomz - Mega Pack (Asst).  They enjoyed coloring the various shapes and figuring out how their scene would be assembled within the aquarium-like structure.  Their particular set had a jungle scene, an aquarium scene, and a color-your-own blank shapes scene.  The toy involves coloring various thick paper cut-outs with the provided color markers, inserting them into stands, and then filling the stands with a liquid provided in single-use packets.  There seemed to be enough packets provided for the projects.  The liquid is slowly absorbed by the paper, causing the colors to blend in sort of a tie-dye effect, with colored crystals forming along the edges of the paper cut-outs.The whole effect is very pretty, but is very fragile.  Any touch will cause the crystals to fall off the paper, ditto a strong vibration hitting the surface the aquarium-like structure is on.  And once the project is completed and the oohs-and-aahs have occurred, the kids lost interest in it because it had to be displayed in a place other than a dresser or a bookcase in their bedroom because of the fragility.It's a cute toy and the kids had fun creating it.  With three scenes to create and time to admire them, the toy does last a bit.  But that is outweighed by how careful you have to be with the finished product.  Given the price of toys today, the current Amazon price of $21.99 is a little too high, in my opinion.  To me, this is more of a $13 toy.

reviewText: I really did want to like this kit.  I thought this would make a sweet gift for my daughter's 9th birthday, since she loves to bake and frequently helps with cooking. I was happy to find a way that would satisfy her interest in baking, eating, and crafts, and I was looking forwarded to seeing her create adorable concoctions.Not so much.Although my daughter can easily follow a cookie or cake recipe from a regular cookbook, the instructions in this kit were hard to follow and confusing. reviewText: Let me preface this review by saying I have never been a big fan of Monopoly. But I sat down to play this the other day - three of us, including my 7-year-old son) and it was quite enjoyable. We all had a good time, my son most of all.One advantage of the electronic banking version is that the game goes faster. Slow Monopoly games are not at all engaging and I quickly lose interest. Moving from player to player more rapidly removes a level of boredom from the game. One disadvantage is that kids won't get anything educational about money out of the game because the banking unit does all the math for you. You also have to trust the person acting as banker to enter all information accurately, since you're not counting you own money, or the other players. Even a mistake could hurt you so it's not just dishonesty but carelessness that could ruin a game. I am well aware of how cut-throat some people can be with regard to this game.One remedy for this might be to place the unit on the board where all players can see it and then enter the amounts being credited and debited.I haven't played Monopoly for years and I did enjoy the new pieces, the skateboard, race car, jumbo jet, cell phone, roller blade, and cheeseburger, though the latter looked more like a thimble to me. I think they could have found something better than a cheeseburger. I like to think there is something more representative (and healthier) of the modern world, like maybe an I-Pad or a laptop computer or a television.Another complaint I have is the symbol used for money, an "M" with two horizontal lines through it as if in mockery of a $ sign. Why they didn't simply use a $ sign I don't know. Seeing "M 1.5M" seems ridiculous - why not just "$ 1.5M" like we'd use in the real world? It may seem a petty gripe but it bothered me.Otherwise, everything is as I'd have expected except for higher rents and costs, to make the old game more modern, and a few modern changes to the community chest and chance cards most folks who have played the game more recently than I are probably already used to. Suffice it to say, if you already like Monopoly you will like Electronic Banking Monopoly.

reviewText: I know a toy is a winner when my seven-year-old daughter gets up early, on a weekday, to play with it. Such was the case with this Barbie set.The decals go on easy enough that with only a little instruction she could decorate the clothing on her own. We were able to wrestle the clothing she decorated on and off the doll and the designs still look like my little fashion maven intended.Mattel has come up with a really neat idea here, I think. If your child likes crafts or fashion then this set is sure to please.My one complaint with this set, and it is common for me, is the packaging. Something like this really shouldn’t require so many fasteners. (The ties are the most annoying, because they require cutting, and a deft hand to remove without damaging the toy.) Seriously, toy companies, look at what Green Toys has done, and do likewise.

reviewText: This is good fun as both a toy and a game, although there's not that much to it. It's the kind of thing you play for a little while, then put down. But with its multiple modes of play and multiplayer games, it won't stay on the shelf forever.There are good and bad points. Bad is the fact that it's loud and annoying; good is the headphone jack. Bad is the fact that the Shake It sensor can be tricky and frustrating for younger kids; good is the fact that the Shake It sensor can be folded into the unit, causing it to be skipped entirely. Good is the nice selection of game modes; bad is the fact that in order to unlock each one other than the basic "tell you what to do" mode, you have to reach a score of 100 in the previous mode. At around a second per move that doesn't sound like much, but it takes a LOT of patience and practice to string that many moves together without messing up. Note that you don't have to unlock the multiplayer games, just the instruction variations (for example, where it tells you the color of the control to hit rather than the name).This reminds me of the old "Simon" game, but far more sophisticated. The classics stick around, even if they change with the times. It's still simple and fun. You won't play it for two straight hours, but you'll probably try it again tomorrow.

reviewText: Bananagrams is a great game for everyone, kids & adults, who can spell and arrange words cross-word style.  And it doesn't matter how many different levels of readers / spellers are playing.  Since you're creating your own board, you're competing against yourself.With it's yellow banana-shaped carrying bag, Bananagrams stows in your purse or backpack to take along everywhere!  I love travel games that still have full-sized playing pieces.All players start with the same number of face-down letters, someone says "split" and players begin creating their own Scrabble-style layout with their letters.  When anyone runs out of tiles, she says "peel" and everyone draws another tile.  You can always "dump" a tile, but you'll have to draw three!  When there are less tiles left than players, the game continues until someone uses all their letters and calls "Bananas!" She is the winner... unless someone challenges one of her words.  The dictionary can confirm any "rotten bananas" and the rest of the players may a chance at the win.If you need to adjust the difficulty, you could level the playing field: limit stronger players to longer words, or give the weaker players a little extra time at the start of the game.Bananagrams is great fun for adults and kids, mixed age groups, anyone who can spell.  We do keep a dictionary around to double-check those rotten bananas.We LOVE Bananagrams!

reviewText: I love Tonka. Just the name beams me back to my childhood. Remember the old Tonka commercial where an elephant steps on a Tonka dump truck? (Look up: Elephant Stepped On A Tonka Toy Hasbro TV Commercial 1970's.) That's why I'm a little disappointed with the TONKA RICOCHET R/C RAMPAGE FLIP.No, it would not survive an encounter with a pesky pachyderm, but it is very tough. I really like the physical TONKA RICOCHET R/C RAMPAGE FLIP, and everyone in the family likes chasing the pets with it. The steering is a bit awkward with a lever for the left wheels a lever for the right wheels, but everyone gets used to it quickly. Smashing it into walls and making it flip is great fun. The remote even has a button that makes the little car do it's tricks. So what's not to like?One word: infrared (IR). Tonka made the unit controlled by an infrared signal instead of a radio signal. The difference is that infrared needs line-of-sight to work. Think about your remote. For most remotes (the ones that use infrared), you have to point the thing directly at the TV or cable box. But some use radio waves, which allows you to point the remote at the ceiling, your boyfriends eyeball, the cat's...you get the idea. So imagine what happens when this little IR-controlled car zooms under the couch. That's right. You're on your hands and knees fishing it out. What's worse is that even on an open floor, it will stop dead after about 10 feet (I'm estimating) because the IR receiver in the car is where the driver would be. As the car zooms away from you, the receiver gets blocked by the body of the car and the car stops. It's very frustrating and a real wet blanket.So while I have respect for the Minnetonka toy manufacturer, and I really like the design of the TONKA RICOCHET R/C RAMPAGE FLIP, the IR design ruins it for me.

reviewText: I bought this ride on because my son loves to bounce and I thought this would be perfect for him. We have had this for almost two months and I am just not very happy with it. My one year old is still not walking yet, so it might get a little better in the future; however, I do regret purchasing this.First, the toy feels super cheap. The plastic is very light and the wheels are wobbly and I feel like they might fall off at any moment. It does not glide smoothly at all whether you use it on hardwood or carpet. I know I didn't pay much for it, but I guess I was expecting it to be a little more substantial. We have another ride on (identified further down) that didn't cost very much more and is much better quality.The bouncing ball is hard to move. I have tried emptying some of the air, but it does not seem to get much better. My son barely makes a dent in it when sitting as hard as he can. This may become easier when he gains some weight, right now he is 20 pounds and pretty light for his age. The kickstand is an interesting feature, but again we have to wait until he gains enough oomph in his bounce to really utilize it.Aside from the un-bounce-able ball and the little swinging monkey, there is nothing engaging or fun on the toy. There are a few little melodies that play on occasion, but nothing else to press or activate.The handlebar is a little awkward and my son has a hard time trying to move himself forward. He also finds it extremely difficult to use it as a push toy, which is what he really loves to do right now being a little afraid to walk on his own. There is also no place for an adult to push unless you are on your hands and knees grasping the very bottom.For Christmas my son just received the "FP Music Parade Ride On" and it is everything this toy isn't. I strongly suggest checking that one out instead.

reviewText: Easy Bake Microwave and Style Deluxe Delights / B003I85V00I really wanted to like this Easy Bake kit - if they hadn't already had me at "fun" and "educational", they would have had me at "mini cakes". I mean, the toy sells itself - I like cakes, I like miniature cakes, and I like things that cook in the microwave (fast!) and require little cleanup. But this toy is such an epic fail on so many levels, I don't know where to begin.1. (Not) Educational: I guess I should have read the description a little more closely, but I sort of thought that this would include recipes for your own cake mixes, once you had used up the mixes that were provided for you. In my naivete, I forgot that including something like that would hurt the resale numbers for the mixes. So, trust me, your kids will learn nothing about baking from this kit - there's zero room for creativity - just add water. The kids won't even learn measurements, because the mixes call for the non-standard measurements that come with the kit, each one marked by a symbol. (So, yes, if you lose the measurement tool, you have to replace it. Joy.)2. (Not) Cheap: Remember how I said that you have to use the Easy Bake brand mixes with this kit, and when you run out you have to buy more? This might be a good time to point out that the mixes that came in my kit were: 2 cake mixes, 3 cookie mixes, and...6 decoration mixes (icing, sprinkles, etc.). That's a nice trick - after a mere 6 mini cakes, it's going to be, "MOMMMM! We need more mixes!!"3. (Not) Sustainable: This kit comes with over a dozen cheap plastic "cooking tools" that are supposedly needed for cooking. Getting past the issues with plastic breaking down into foods when microwaved, it's worth noting that most of these plastic toys are (a) choking hazards, (b) going to clutter the nursery considerably, (c) superfluous to the whole process, and (d) custom sizes that will have to be replaced when lost (for instance, the measurement spoons). Everyone's trying to be green-conscious now - would it have killed the company to include standard measurements so that you don't have to buy MORE plastic junk when the first batch inevitably breaks or gets lost? Teaspoons and tablespoons aren't a new thing.4. (Not) Fun: You'd think they'd at least have this down, but the first thing you'll notice when you make your first "mix" (and make it count - you only have 2 cake mixes, after all), is that this kit is the exact opposite of "easy". The mix bubbled up in an ugly fashion in the microwave, leaving cakes that looked like they had boils. Then getting the cakes out intact was a nightmare - the cakes kept trying to slump over and break and keep in mind that you only get three cakes per mix, so if you want to get the most out of your mix, then all three really need to be perfect. All three cakes can only be lifted out of the molds at the same time, so you can't even coax them out one at a time to maximize your odds of success. Enjoy the "fun"!5. (Not) Tasty: I like to say I've yet to meet a chocolate cake I didn't like, but in order to keep saying that, I need to either suffer amnesia after using this kit, or I have to reclassify the output as something other than "cake". Seriously, this stuff is brown-colored spongy yuck. It's not even bland, it's aggressively disgusting. There's something so off about the taste and texture, that I couldn't even finish the third "mini" cake - the only way I got as far as I did was to pop the first one in my mouth, gag and decide to nibble on the second one, and ultimately throw the third one away. How hard is it to get these mixes right? This isn't rocket science.Ultimately, I can't think of anything redeeming about this kit. If your kids just want to play with the microwave to make yummy snacks, I'd recommend going the MUCH cheaper (and greener, and more appetizing, and less likely to choke your toddler on plastic bits, etc.) route of buying someBetty Crocker Warm Delightsbowls, levering them gently onto a plate, and letting the kids go nuts with some frosting in a can, a laPillsbury Easy Frost Vanilla Dream. Going such a route will also be much easier to cleanup, so everyone wins, really.~ Ana Mardoll

Our daughter is still on the young side, but already enjoys "cooking," so we got these instead of metal (which are what the KidKraft matching set is) or plastic pots and pans because they quite frankly look better and seemed higher quality. Love the wooden utensils and oven mitt that come with the set, too!

I never got around to giving it away and my 2 year old does play with it sometimes while I'm in the shower. reviewText: My eight year old Son and ten year old Daughter both love the Hot Wheels Sky Jump Track Set. It's really cool to watch and play with and I myself am amazed at well it works most of the time. It includes one car that you put on a diving board. You release the car and it falls into a bowl and into a tunnel that flips your car onto its wheels. Then a set of wheels will propel the car through a twisting track and a second set of wheels will send the car flying into the bowl again. The entire process only takes a few seconds and it will work time and time again with an occasional time where the car will land on the track upside down or get stuck on the track or tube. It's designed and made fairly well and unless you abuse it then it should hold up quite well. The only bad thing that I can think of is how noisy it is. It's quite loud and after hearing it for 10 minutes it starts to get annoying. It even scares our two dogs and will chase them upstairs. Other than that it's a great track and I think most kids will love it.
summary: My kids love it, works really well but is really loud

reviewText: I have a 4 year old and 1 year old and they love this toy.  Cheap batteries don't last in this toy, you need the super high quality ones.  As for butterflies not coming out, it works just fine with new batteries.  You may have to bend the wings out a bit.  They come folded in one direction, just flip them the other way, so they open up and look more like butterflies.  The trunk stays up if you bring it up manually after turning it on and it will stay up even after turning it off.  Don't use it on soft carpet because the unit will not turn on that way.  You can solve that problem by placing a book underneath, though.  My only recommendation is that they include more butterflies.UPDATE:My oldest is now 8.  The kids still enjoy this toy at the grandparents' house.  It has lasts many years and both my children and my niece and nephew enjoy it.  The trunk is getting worn but I'd say we've gotten our money's worth.

reviewText: The Ravensburger Xoomy Animals set is a unique children's introduction to drawing. It comes with 20 different transparent animal images which your children will be able to learn to copy/trace. 10 sheets of paper, and a black felt tip pen. The Xoomy allows you to mix and match these different images as well as magnify to create small picture or larger ones. The Xoomy is recommended for children ages 7+ however, my 5 year old daughter is quite able to use this on her own and loves it. In fact she quickly ran out of paper (10 isn't a lot) so I had to get some of my basic white printer paper and cut her some more.You can also buy other stencils for it includes a boy's pattern and girls pattern set. It does require 4 AA batteries which are not included, but other than that it is ready to go straight out of the box.Overall this is a unique toy that will help stimulate your child's artistic imagination.

reviewText: First, let me admit that our twin toddlers have spent relatively little time watching Elmo on-screen.  We promote little screen time in our house, and Sesame Street represents only a portion of that time.  So before receiving this gift, they probably didn't really know Elmo well, and as a result, I didn't expect them to "connect" with the toy immediately.Certainly, their love of this toy is not becuase it's Elmo whom they have a relationship with because they see him on TV all of the time.  They love the toy because it's a loveable toy!After receiving this gift, they connected with Elmo immediately.  One of them seems to have claimed Elmo for his own; he now loves to carry Elmo around in "hug" pose - and Elmo is nearly as large as he is!  He also may have a future as a dentist, as another favorite activity is examining Elmo's open mouth while Elmo lies down for a nap.When we initially saw this toy, I was somewhat concerned about durability as the motorized arms are long and spindly.  But a few days into our experience, the toy seems to be holding up well and we have not seen any danger of breakage.We love the variety of interactions available in this toy - it sings several songs, and has a "hugging" mode, a "sleeping" mode, and even offers feedback when carried improperly - it turns out that Elmo likes to be carried upright, and asks for this when he is carried upside-down!On the down side, the twin who is not currently holding this Elmo is not always pleased - this has prompted an additional purchase of a 3 1/2-year-old red monster.

reviewText: This game is fairly straightforward.  It comes with four sets of six differently-colored small blocks, three natural color blocks, a supply of cardboard "chips" and a deck of cards which are yellow on one side and red on the other.  The yellow cards each show a structure of three or four blocks while the red cards show a structure of five or six blocks.  At the command of the "Master Builder" (which rotates each round), each player grabs his or her blocks and attempts to assemble the structure shown on the card.  Upon completing the structure, the players reach for one of the natural colored blocks in the center of the table - note, there is one less block than there are players.  If, in your haste to grab a natural colored block, you knock down your structure, you have to put down the natural colored block and rebuild your structure before attempting to grab the block again (this happens more often than you might think).  Once all the natural colored blocks are gone, the Master Builder inspects each players' work.  Each player who has correctly completed the structure gets a cardboard chip.  Each such player who also has a natural colored block gets an extra chip.  The first player to reach 10 chips wins.I played this last night with my daughters, ages almost 4 and almost 6.  While it was fun for a while, it is really too easy for the targeted age (5+).  Both my girls were able to do the yellow cards easily, so we quickly switched to the red cards.  My older daughter still found them to be too easy, while even my younger daughter was able to do most of them.As you might guess, however, it is difficult to balance fair play among players of different ages due to different levels of motor coordination.  The instructions come with some variations to account for varying levels of coordination, such as having any adults use red cards while children use yellow cards, and/or restricting adults to one hand only.  These are helpful, but you might still encounter difficulty if you have more than two different skill sets.  Overall, I'd recommend this game for groups of same age children.A good feature about this game is that it can be played on multiple levels.  My older daughter is highly competitive and she really enjoyed the race for the natural block (and the hilarity of knocking over the structure in the process, especially when I did it).  My younger daughter, on the other hand, does not enjoy competitive games and she got rather frustrated after a while.  At that point we played just to see who could build the structure without worrying about timing.  At this level it is very helpful for developing visual-spatial problem solving and hand-eye coordination for younger children.  Finally, my daughters just started building their own structures using all the blocks and working together very cooperatively.  They tried to build the tallest tower or the sturdiest building, and they tried to make various patterns.As with all Ravensburger products, this game is pretty durable, although with younger children there's probably a good chance of cards and/or chips getting lost.  The game is also educational, which is probably a plus for most parents.  As far as fun, it is for a while.  We played for a total of about half an hour, only about ten minutes of which were spent on the actual competitive game.  My older daughter seemed to grow bored with the cards after a while, and I don't anticipate her getting this game out terribly often.  I am considering looking into the older version of the game, as I think this one is too easy for her.  My younger daughter enjoyed making the structures on the cards, and continued at it for quite a while.  I will probably get this game out more with her to use on a non-competitive basis.

reviewText: The Fisher-Price Servin' Surprises Kitchen & Table is a nice addition for those little chefs who want to do some pretend-play in their kitchen, but it also friendly to families who are hard-up for space (like we are). Basically the Servin' Surprises Kitchen & Table does double duty as both a kitchen, and as a standard table, and does a good job at both.Assembly was quick and fairly easy, taking roughly half an hour to go from a pile of plastic pieces (14) and screws (24) to the completed product. The table seems very sturdy once completed and is a good height for my toddler at the higher setting (with the "oven" attached; the lower setting seems practically useless).In "kitchen mode," the stovetop basically makes three sounds, bubbling, boiling on the burner, sizzling on the grill and the ticking and "ding" of the oven timer (along with a red light in the oven itself). It's simple, but it works, and my daughter likes turning the knobs while she pretends to cook. Turn the stovetop over, and you have a flat table-top and then the Servin' Surprises table looks very much like any other toddler/play-table out there. You can take the oven off as well, but we just leave it there, as I would imagine most would.Another plus with the Servin' Surprises table is that it comes with a lot of accessories: the "Magical" serving tray, cookies to bake (with cookie sheet), a pizza that can go from veggie to pepperoni and plates, cups, forks, etc. ("service for two," as the description calls it). Fisher-Price also makes Servin' Surprises add-on items for the Servin' Surprises Kitchen, so you can expand that a good bit (my daughter will be getting the Tea Party Set for Christmas). I like the fact that you can life the center piece off to reveal a storage compartment for the accessories.Overall, we've been very satisfied with this table, but there are a couple of things that stop it from being flawless. The oven door is difficult to open and close, just about requiring an adult to do it (and even then, it takes some fiddling to get it to close properly). The door of the oven has no "glass," so it's just an open hole, which was a bit disappointing, and the pizza pan very barely fits in the oven. The table also doesn't come with chairs (and doesn't claim to), but it would be nice if Fisher Price offered some that were made for it. The lack of batteries (requires 6AA batteries between the stovetop and serving tray) isn't surprising to me (seems like nothing comes with batteries these days), but it would have been nice had they been included. Remember to buy some...Those things are minor quibbles, and all-in-all, the Fisher Price Servin' Surprises Kitchen & Table is a great addition. My daughter loves it, the price isn't bad for all that you get and I just like the fact that we can use it as a standard table for playing with other toys, drawing, etc. when kitchen playtime is over.
summary: Great multipurpose table (and not a bad kitchen for little chefs).

reviewText: This game is unbelievably simple to learn: roll a die, set a timer, turn over a card and start building.  After opening the box, my 5 and 7-year-old and I were playing in less than 5 minutes.  The beauty of this game is that you can play it according to the rules or make some modifications to play with younger children.  You may want to give children under the age of 8 more time to build, or the easier cards. Likewise, adults playing with children need less time or more challenges.  I see this as a game that becomes even more fun to play as my kids get older.Because there's an element of luck in rolling the die and shuffling the cards, no two games are ever alike.  You only play 4 rounds to determine a winner, so games are long enough to be fun, but not so long that they're frustrating or tiring.An excellent game for learning how to copy patterns build from a plan.  Like any good educational game, it's makes learning fun.

reviewText: This toy has been great for helping my daughter learn how to better use her fine motor skills.  I think the toy was designed to have different levels of strength and coordination needed to pop up each one of the animals.  This would make sense, as it provides additional value for the children.  What good would the toy be if it only developed one specific motor skill?  Eventually my daughter was able to master activating each one of the animals, and it took about 5-6 months.  We got it for her when she was about 8 months old.  The easiest one for her to master was the circle button (panda), as it requires only a simple press.  The second one she mastered was the left to right slider (giraffe), although at first she could only operate it when the it when sliding it from right to left, as she has to use the edge of the toy to get enough leverage to move the slider.  Third was the rocking switch (monkey), which is similar to the slider switch, albeit slightly different and requiring a bit different type of coordination to activate.  Fourth was the up and down switch (elephant).  She was able to master pulling the switch down fairly quickly, but learning to push it up took a bit longer.  Finally, the turn-key switch (lion) was the last to be mastered.  It requires a good amount of force at the end to activate the pop-up mechanism, but I don't think that's a bad thing.  I think it helps the children progress as they are developing, learning step by step.The only "negative" I have found with this is that if you drop it, sometimes the toys pop up.  It has survived a plethora of droppings, and is quite durable.  All the switches still work perfectly.
summary: Great strength and coordination building tool for 8-24 months

On the new Leaptop you can personalize by pressing the p and m buttons at the same time and then typing in the child's name. Then the Leaptop will spell your child's name anytime they press the letter that starts their name. That's it.The old version you had to connect to a computer but you could select the child's name, Scout or Violet would say their name, spell it and sing a song. You could select which songs you wanted it to play and you could personalize emails to/from Mommy, Daddy, Grandma, Nana, Grammy, Grandpa Robert or thousands of names and other selections.So ignore all the wonderful reviews that you see on amazon about the great personalization features. If you want a little laptop for your child then look for a used one in the old version. And whatever you do, don't let them play with it if they have a stomach bug.

There aren't a lot of extra pieces for the kids to lose which is a huge plus.  The house doesn't have a lot of snapped in parts to break and fall off. The dolls all fit inside, and the house folds up neatly into a corner.  Goes from a nice sized house to compact storage very easily.I'm sure your younger girls will enjoy this dollhouse as much as mine.

reviewText: Party Gras is an interesting game and I certainly don't own any games like it. Unlike most games that require a minimum of 2-3 players for optimal play with Party Gras the opposite is true. The more people you have playing the more fun it is, and because it can accommodate such a large number of players nobody ever has to feel left out or like they have to team up with another player just to make sure everybody can play. (Which is one of my biggest complaints at game night is having to play something like Settlers of Catan on a team.)Party Gras has a simple enough premise: Get all the beads you can (just like Mardi Gras)! But how you get those beads is what makes this game such a riot. Along with the strands of beads that every player starts out with each player is given a card with a task that they either must do or convince another player to do. Once their card has been completed they show it to another player and receive a strand of their beads in exchange.This game is great for large family gatherings if you're a loud, boisterous, outgoing family; ice breakers for small conferences and group settings; and at any type of party. Also, the game is super flexible because you can play until somebody has ALL the beads (which I honestly think might be impossible if your friends and family are as competitive as mine are) or you can have a predetermined time limit for the game and whoever has the most beads at the end of that time period is the winner.Overall it's a fun game and great if you've got a large group to play with.
summary: Great Party Game! Excellent for Large Groups!

reviewText: This little toy is really pretty amazing, especially for the price. It is very thin and light, which is just perfect for this age, as most of the toys are bigger and bulky. It's actually a touch screen, and the kids get that concept right away. It sings and talks, of course, but what struck me most of all was that it is "smart."My 2-year-old was playing with it, and it was asking her to touch a particular picture ("3 blueberries" or similar). Instead of touching the picture it was asking for, she kept touching another picture. The toy caught up with her after she did this 3 or 4 times, and instead asked her to touch the picture she was already pressing over and over. Now, it was clear she didn't understand what the toy was asking her to do, so this change in tactics may have helped her to understand. My 5-year-old, of course, got the idea of the toy right away, and was able to do the games. He's out of the age range of this toy, but it still kept him entertained for a few minutes.I don't think we've even found everything that this little toy can do yet. My 2-year-old doesn't play with it for long periods of time, but I think it might make a good travel toy, because it is so light and easy to transport. It doesn't seem flimsy, but my kids are gentle with their toys for the most part, so I can't speak to it's durability yet, especially with kids who are more physical.
